reason: The sources provide multi-site backing for over a dozen unique claims about Charon's discovery, physical properties, orbital dynamics, and barycenter.
story: In 1978, astronomer James Christy was examining photographic plates of Pluto when he noticed something strange: Pluto looked elongated. Re-examining older plates, he realized the bulge moved in a steady 6.387-day cycle. It was not a defect, but a giant moon that he named Charon, partly after his wife Charlene. Charon turned out to be massive relative to Pluto, stretching roughly half Pluto's diameter. Because Charon is so heavy, Pluto doesn't simply pull Charon around itself. Instead, the center of gravity of the Pluto-Charon system—the barycenter—lies in empty space outside of Pluto. Both worlds orbit this invisible point in space every 6.4 days, locked face-to-face in mutual tidal synchronization. When NASA's New Horizons spacecraft flew past in July 2015, it captured close-up images of this pair, confirming one of the most unusual gravitational dances in the Solar System.
angle: Pluto and its giant moon Charon orbit a point of empty space located entirely outside of Pluto itself.

claims.claim: James Christy discovered Pluto's moon Charon in 1978 using photographic plates taken at the US Naval Observatory Flagstaff Station.
Christy noticed Pluto appeared elongated on photographic plates, which led to Charon's discovery.
Christy proposed the name Charon partly as a tribute to his wife Charlene, whose nickname was Char.
Charon is the largest of Pluto's five natural satellites.
Charon's diameter is roughly half that of Pluto.
Charon has roughly one-eighth (12%) of Pluto's mass, making it unusually heavy relative to its parent body.
The center of mass (barycenter) of the Pluto-Charon system lies in open space outside Pluto.
Pluto and Charon are mutually tidally locked, meaning each body permanently shows the exact same face to the other.
Pluto and Charon complete an orbit around their common barycenter every 6.387 days.
Pluto and Charon underwent a series of mutual eclipses and transits starting in early 1985 that confirmed Charon's existence.
Clyde Tombaugh discovered Pluto in 1930 at the Lowell Observatory while searching for Percival Lowell's hypothetical Planet X.
NASA's New Horizons spacecraft conducted the first flyby of Pluto and Charon in July 2015.
The International Astronomical Union formally reclassified Pluto as a dwarf planet in August 2006.
Pluto has five known satellites: Charon, Styx, Nix, Kerberos, and Hydra.

disputed: Charon's exact mass ratio to Pluto: older reports state Charon is about 22% of Pluto's mass, whereas modern satellite dynamics measurements specify approximately 12.2% (0.1218:1). A script should attribute updated measurements or use 'roughly one-eighth'.

Charon's exact diameter: source values range from ~1,172 km to 1,212 km based on different occultations and flyby data. A script should state 'just over half of Pluto's diameter' rather than declaring a single exact kilometer figure without attribution.

Name pronunciation: classical astronomical convention uses a hard /k/ sound, whereas discoverer James Christy and NASA use a soft /ʃ/ sound in honor of Christy's wife Charlene. Script can briefly note both pronunciations exist.
